I've been looking at a correctness and security issue in the Winch baseline compiler's code generation for memory access instructions on 64-bit platforms.

*   When a 32-bit WebAssembly memory address is used for a load or store operation on a 64-bit platform, the Winch compiler backend must zero-extend the 32-bit address to 64-bit before computing the final memory address — not sign-extend it.

*   On AArch64, all memory address computation instructions for 32-bit WebAssembly heaps must use the 32-bit register form (wN) with the unsigned extend word operation (uxtw), instead of the 64-bit register form (xN) with unsigned extend 64-bit (uxtx). This applies to loads, stores, and atomic operations.

*   On x64, before using a 32-bit value as the offset in a 64-bit memory address computation (addq), the compiler must emit an explicit instruction that zero-extends the 32-bit value to 64-bit (e.g., movl %reg32, %reg32). This applies to loads, stores, atomic loads, atomic stores, atomic read-modify-write operations, and all memory-accessing instructions.

*   A WebAssembly module that loads a signed 8-bit value of -1 (0xFF) from memory and then uses that sign-extended i32 value (-1, or 0xFFFFFFFF unsigned) as the base address for a subsequent memory load with an offset must trap with 'out of bounds memory access' rather than succeeding.

*   A WebAssembly module that uses the return value of a table.grow operation (which is -1 if the grow fails) as a memory store address with any offset must trap with 'out of bounds memory access' rather than succeeding.


**CRITICAL:** Do not modify any files in the `tests/` directory.
The verification system will apply test patches automatically.
Your task is to implement the feature in source files only.
I'll start by exploring the Winch compiler codebase to understand its structure and locate the relevant code for memory address computation.

I found detailed information about this security vulnerability. Here's a summary of the Winch baseline compiler bug and its fix:

## The Vulnerability (GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83)

**Impact:** Wasmtime with its Winch (baseline) non-default compiler backend may allow properly constructed guest Wasm to access host memory outside of its linear-memory sandbox. This vulnerability requires use of the Winch compiler (-Ccompiler=winch). By default, Wasmtime uses its Cranelift backend, not Winch.

**Root cause (the sign-extend/zero-extend bug):** The underlying bug assumes a 32-bit memory offset stored in a 64-bit register has its upper bits cleared when it may not, and so closely related variants of the initial proof-of-concept may be able to access truly arbitrary memory in-process.

**Affected architectures:** With Winch, the same incorrect assumption is present in theory on both aarch64 and x86-64. The aarch64 case has an observed-working proof of concept, while the x86-64 case is theoretical and may not be reachable in practice.

**Scope of memory access:** This Winch compiler bug can allow the Wasm guest to access memory before or after the linear-memory region, independently of whether pre- or post-guard regions are configured. The accessible range in the initial bug proof-of-concept is up to 32KiB before the start of memory, or ~4GiB after the start of memory, independently of the size of pre- or post-guard regions or the use of explicit or guard-region-based bounds checking.

**Potential consequences:** This could result in a host process segmentation fault (DoS), an arbitrary data leak from the host process, or with a write, potentially an arbitrary RCE.

## The Fix

Wasmtime 43.0.1, 42.0.2, and 36.0.7 have been released with fixes for this issue.

**Mitigation/Workaround:** There are no workarounds within the Winch compiler backend while using the affected versions. Users of Wasmtime are encouraged either to upgrade to patched versions or, if that is not possible, use the Cranelift compiler backend.

The core of the fix relates to the memory addressing computation: when a 32-bit WebAssembly memory offset is placed into a 64-bit register, the code incorrectly assumed the value would be zero-extended (upper bits cleared) when in fact the value could be sign-extended, allowing the address to point outside the sandboxed linear memory region.

## Overview of GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83

Wasmtime is a runtime for WebAssembly. From 25.0.0 to before 36.0.7, 42.0.2, and 43.0.1, Wasmtime with its Winch (baseline) non-default compiler backend may allow properly constructed guest Wasm to access host memory outside of its linear-memory sandbox. This vulnerability requires use of the Winch compiler (-Ccompiler=winch). By default, Wasmtime uses its Cranelift backend, not Winch.

## The bug (relevant to `bounds.rs` / `load_heap_addr` / `uxtw`)

With Winch, the same incorrect assumption is present in theory on both aarch64 and x86-64. The aarch64 case has an observed-working proof of concept, while the x86-64 case is theoretical and may not be reachable in practice. The connection to the `uxtw` extend operator you're asking about lies in how the aarch64 backend computes the effective heap address. On aarch64, heap loads use a load instruction with a register offset that applies the `uxtw` (unsigned extend word) extension to a 32-bit index — the same pattern visible in Wasmtime's documented objdump output showing an instruction like ldr w2, [x5, w6, uxtw]. The incorrect assumption in the bounds-checking path meant the extended index could reference memory outside the sandbox.

This Winch compiler bug can allow the Wasm guest to access memory before or after the linear-memory region, independently of whether pre- or post-guard regions are configured. The accessible range in the initial bug proof-of-concept is up to 32KiB before the start of memory, or ~4GiB after the start of memory.

## Fix and affected versions

The issue was one of several disclosed together. Four issues were discovered in the Winch backend: GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83, GHSA-f984-pcp8-v2p7, GHSA-q49f-xg75-m9xw, GHSA-m9w2-8782-2946, and two in Cranelift: GHSA-jhxm-h53p-jm7w, GHSA-qqfj-4vcm-26hv.

The advisory was published GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83 · Apr 9, 2026 · wasmtime (Rust) >= 25.0.0, <= 36.0.6, >= 37.0.0, <= 42.0.1, 43.0.0 · 36.0.7, 42.0.2, 43.0.1 — meaning the fix landed in patch releases 36.0.7, 42.0.2, and 43.0.1.

## Summary

I fixed the Winch baseline compiler's correctness/security bug (CVE-2026-34987 / [GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-xx5w-cvp6-jv83), [RUSTSEC-2026-0095](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0095.html)) where a 32-bit Wasm memory index held in a 64-bit register was implicitly assumed to have its upper bits cleared. When the index came from a sign-extended value (e.g. `i32.load8_s` of `0xFF`, or a failed `table.grow` returning `-1`), the stale high bits produced an out-of-sandbox address instead of trapping.

The root cause was in `winch/codegen/src/codegen/bounds.rs`, `load_heap_addr_unchecked`, where the index was added to the heap base using the 64-bit pointer size with no zero-extension. This single site is reached by all memory-accessing instructions (loads, stores, atomic loads/stores, atomic RMW), so fixing it covers every case.

Changes (all in source, none in `tests/`):

1. **`bounds.rs`** — when the target pointer is 64-bit and the heap index type is 32-bit, add the index via a new zero-extending add instead of a plain `add`; otherwise (memory64) keep the plain add.
2. **`masm.rs`** — added `add_uextend` to the `MacroAssembler` trait.
3. **`isa/x64/masm.rs`** — `add_uextend` emits an explicit `movl %reg, %reg` (via the existing `movzx`/`I64Extend32` path) to zero-extend the 32-bit index before the `addq`.
